problems.label: Strong fear and avoidance of one kind of object or situation
definitions: Takes long detours, refuses certain trips or turns down jobs and family events to stay clear of one particular trigger, and leaves quickly if it appears unexpectedly.
Rates fear at 7 or higher out of 10 when near the trigger or picturing it, and describes the body's reaction, for example a racing heart, shaking or an urge to run.
Can name what the avoidance has cost, such as a promotion that required flying, a family visit skipped because of the dog, or a garden left untended because of bees.
Wants to be able to face the trigger, for example to fly to a family wedding, but backs out at the last step even while judging the real risk to be small.
longTermGoals: The client can face the feared object or situation in the ways their life calls for, with fear that is bearable and no longer steers their choices.

shortTermObjectives.text: By session 2, explain in their own words how avoidance and escape keep fear going, and how planned, step-by-step approach lets the brain learn that the trigger is safer or more manageable than predicted.

By session 3, build a fear ladder of at least 8 steps linked to the trigger, rating each for expected fear (0-10) and adding variations such as distance, time, setting and being alone or with someone.

At intake, at week 6 and at the end of treatment, complete a behavioral approach test: move as close to the trigger as the client is willing, and record the closest step reached and peak fear (0-10), to track progress over time.

Over weeks 3 to 10, complete at least 3 planned exposure practices per week (in session and at home), staying until the planned end of each one and writing down the prediction beforehand and what actually happened afterward.

If the client prefers a faster course and the clinician is experienced in it, decide together by session 3 whether to use a single extended exposure session (often up to about 3 hours), followed by a written home-practice plan for the next 4 weeks.

For triggers that are hard to set up in real life (for example flying or storms), use imagined, video or virtual reality exposure steps by week 6 where available, then move to real-life practice as soon as it is practical.
In the final 2 sessions, write a plan to keep the gains, including at least 1 planned contact with the trigger each month for 3 months and what to do if avoidance starts to creep back.

problems.label: Fearful predictions, dread and safety habits that keep the fear going
definitions: Predicts disaster near the trigger (for example 'the dog will attack', 'the plane will crash' or 'I will lose control and fall') and rates these outcomes as very likely even when the real risk is low.
Relies on safety habits near the trigger, such as gripping something, shutting eyes, needing a companion, checking exits, constant distraction or taking a sedating medicine 'just in case'.
Feels dread for days or weeks before an expected encounter (for example before a flight or a trip to the mountains), with poor sleep or trouble focusing.
Feels ashamed or frustrated about the fear and is unsure whether facing it is worth the discomfort.
longTermGoals: The client sees feared outcomes as less likely and more manageable, approaches the trigger without leaning on safety habits, and chooses to face fear for the sake of what matters to them.

shortTermObjectives.text: By session 2, talk through what the client would gain and lose by facing the fear versus keeping things as they are, and rate readiness to start exposure (0-10); if readiness is below 5, revisit by session 4.
By session 3, name at least 1 valued reason for facing the fear (for example visiting family overseas or hiking with a child) and write it on a card to bring to every exposure practice.
Over weeks 3 to 10, before each exposure practice, write the specific feared outcome and how likely it seems (0-100); afterward, record what happened and re-rate how likely it now seems.
By week 4, list at least 3 safety habits used near the trigger, then drop or cut back at least 1 of them each week during practices through week 10, noting what was learned each time.

For 4 weeks, when dread about an upcoming encounter shows up, use a brief step-back or mindful noticing skill (for example labeling the thought as 'a prediction') at least once a day, rating how much the dread gets in the way (0-10).

If worry reaches well beyond the one trigger, complete the GAD-7 at intake and every 4 weeks to track broader anxiety, and discuss with the clinician whether a wider anxiety plan is needed; for the phobia itself, rely on fear ratings and the approach test.

problems.label: Fear of blood, needles or medical procedures that gets in the way of health care
definitions: Has put off or missed needed medical, dental or vaccine visits, blood tests or procedures because of fear of needles, blood, injury or medical settings.
Has fainted, nearly fainted, or felt light-headed and pale when seeing blood, needles or injuries, or even when thinking about them.
Avoids related TV, conversations or helping an injured family member.
Feels embarrassed about the reaction and may not have told health care providers about it.
longTermGoals: The client gets the medical and dental care they need, using skills that prevent or reduce fainting, with fear at a bearable level.

shortTermObjectives.text: By session 2, review fainting history and health conditions (for example heart problems or pregnancy) and, with the client's consent, check with a medical provider before blood or needle exposure if needed; plan the first steps so the client is seated or lying down.

If the client tends to faint, by session 4 learn and practice a muscle-tensing skill that briefly raises blood pressure (applied tension), several times a day for 1 week, then use it during exposure steps. Relaxation-only skills are generally not used during blood or needle exposure for clients who faint.

Over weeks 3 to 10, work up a blood and needle ladder (for example pictures, then videos, then handling medical supplies, then watching a finger-prick, then a blood draw), completing at least 2 steps a week and rating fear and faintness (each 0-10).

By week 8, role-play telling a health care provider about the fear and asking for helpful changes (for example lying down for a blood draw or a short pause before the needle), then use that script at the next real appointment.

By week 12, book and attend at least 1 needed medical, dental or vaccine appointment that has been put off, using the planned coping steps, and review with the clinician what went well and what to adjust.

collaborativeNote: These are starting points for clinician review, not a finished plan, and they do not diagnose (see DSM-5-TR and ICD-11; the clinician decides any diagnosis and rules out medical causes and other anxiety conditions). Rewrite every goal and objective with the client in their own words, let the client choose which steps to take and when, and record their agreement before anything goes into the plan. Exposure targets only fears that are out of proportion to real danger; respect realistic caution (for example venomous animals, unsafe heights or places where the client could face harassment), and do not ask the client to enter genuinely unsafe settings. Fear of the same trigger can carry different meanings across cultures and faiths, so ask before building the ladder. Faith-integrated versions of the linked interventions are used only when the client asks for them and gives informed consent. If thoughts of suicide or self-harm come up, the clinician assesses directly and plans safety with the client; crisis contacts are 988 (call or text, US), the local emergency number and findahelpline.com. Do not add names or other identifying details. Resource only. Not a substitute for clinical judgment.
